questions.question: How can I register?
questions.answer: Registration on the Check It Out platform is simple. Just click the "Sign up" button in the top right corner of the page, choose the account type (business or influencer), and then fill out the registration form. After data verification, you can use all the platform's features.

questions.question: How do influencers settle payments with companies?
questions.answer: Payments are made according to the terms outlined in the specific listing. Check It Out does not mediate payments; however, our platform monitors whether both parties have fulfilled the previously agreed terms. In the event of reported fraud, the affected party can rely on full support from the Check It Out team.

questions.question: How does the collaboration system work? As an influencer, do I have access to all offers?
questions.answer: As an influencer, you have access to all offers for which your account meets the requirements (e.g., location, number of followers).

questions.question: Does submitting an application for collaboration automatically mean its acceptance?
questions.answer: No, your application must be accepted by the company that posted it. The company has the option to review your profile, statistics, and previous collaborations, and then decides whether to accept your application. After the company accepts your application, you must also confirm the terms of the collaboration.

oss.title: checkItOut is open source under MIT — the backend, the greenfield frontend, and the method that built them
oss.story: We are opening the code and sharing what we learned: we want Polish and EU companies to focus on their business — and take our platform as the blueprint that handles all the rest.
oss.pentest: We had the platform independently penetration-tested — GrayBox, OWASP methodology, by WRO4digITal (EDIH Wrocław, with the Wrocław Centre for Networking and Supercomputing). It came back with an above-average security posture and a short, honest list of findings.

velocity.title: Speed is a feedback loop
velocity.subtitle: Why a strongly-typed backend, generated frontend types under strict TypeScript, and an AI teammate that reads both runtimes' logs compound into velocity.
velocity.loopsLabel: Three loops decide velocity — good architecture demotes bugs to faster loops

compile.d: tsc strict + Angular strictTemplates. A renamed BE field, a nulled DTO, a widened enum — the generated client changes and the build goes red before any human or agent even runs the app.

suite.d: The pre-commit gate: the fourteen-step check:full — eleven audit scripts, both typechecks, ng build strictTemplates, 1,141 unit specs. What the compiler can't see — envelope translation, i18n parity, fixture coverage — dies here, still before a commit exists.

runtime.d: pm2 tails BE :8080 and both FEs; trace-equivalence replays the same flows against legacy and rewrite. The truth the first two loops can't reach — timing, headers, real data — is one log read away.

velocity.loopsMoral: Every architectural choice above moves a bug class from a slow loop to a faster one. That is the whole trick.
velocity.contractRef: The full type journey — one generated symbol, three consumers, drift dead at compile time — is the Contract card above.

stats.icse: of shipped JavaScript bugs are detectable by TypeScript — measured on real public bug fixes (ICSE 2017; the authors call it conservative).
stats.airbnb: of Airbnb's production postmortem bugs were preventable by TypeScript — but only when used strictly. Strict mode is not a preference; it is the feature.
stats.agents: of code contributions already involve coding agents (large-scale GitHub study, 2026) — the constraint has moved from writing code to verifying it.

velocity.researchSources: Sources: Gao, Bird & Barr, “To Type or Not to Type”, ICSE 2017 · Bunge, Airbnb postmortem analysis, JSConf Hawaii 2019 · Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025 · large-scale agent-contribution studies, 2026.

agent.headline: An autonomous agent is exactly as fast as its verifier
agent.intro: Agent research keeps landing on one line: feedback only catches what the verifier can see. So we spent the rewrite building the verifier. The typed contract refutes wrong code in seconds, the gate refutes wrong behaviour in seconds more, and the logs refute wrong assumptions at runtime — which is why an agent can work here for hours without drifting.

refute.d: Strict tsc + strictTemplates turn the whole BE contract into a compile-time oracle: the agent's wrong guess fails in seconds, not in QA.

logs.d: The agent tails BE and FE logs via pm2 while it clicks the app in a real browser — runtime truth closes the loop static checks can't.

graph.d: Iterations, commits, lessons and open bugs live in a Neo4j graph (147 iterations deep), so session N+1 starts where session N stopped — not from zero.

agent.pullQuote: Feedback only catches what the verifier can see — so we made the verifier see everything.

method.headline: Break it at compile time. Never in production.
method.intro: checkItOut is live — real users, a real Stripe billing pipeline behind them — so the legacy UI comes out one route at a time, never in a big bang. The whole rewrite is engineered so a mistake surfaces as a red build on our machine, not a broken page on a customer's.

types.d: Strong Java types on the backend compile into an OpenAPI 3 contract — 41 services, 181 models, real string enums — that generates the TypeScript Angular client. Feature code is forbidden from touching that client directly (gate G2); it goes through strict-mode wrapper services instead. The same generated types flow into both the Angular service layer and the Cucumber step definitions, so a changed backend field stops the frontend compiling — Gherkin included — long before it reaches a user.

pyramid.d: The frontend stacks five layers: L0 type-level contract assertions that ride the compiler, L1 service tests that mock the client and check the request envelope, L2 component, L3 BDD run by playwright-bdd, and L4 byte-stable visual baselines plus legacy-vs-greenfield pixel parity — all drawing from one shared fixture source. Underneath sits the backend's own three-tier pyramid: unit, integration on Testcontainers Postgres and Redis, and end-to-end Cucumber.

slice.d: Every change starts as design-first brainstorming, fans out to parallel recon, critique and judge agents, and lands as one slice per commit — a single user-visible change with its tests, i18n, fixture and visual baseline together. A multi-step husky pre-commit gate reverts on the first red, while trace-equivalence checks fingerprint legacy-vs-greenfield API calls to catch drift the compiler can't. The BDD corpus, ported straight from the backend, is the executable oracle.

faster.d: It reads like more ceremony up front; it is less total work. Every bug a gate catches is a production incident that never happens — and the research is blunt about the trade: test-first discipline adds a modest slice of effort up front and buys back far more in defects that never ship.

method.pullQuote: A backend schema change can't quietly reach a customer. It breaks our build first — the Gherkin too.
method.metrics: Lighthouse: best-practices 100 · SEO 100 · accessibility 100 · CLS 0.018 · total blocking time 50 ms. We quote these, not a headline performance score — the perf number rides a simulated slow-4G throttle.
method.research: Grounded, not decorative: Gao, Bird & Barr (ICSE 2017) measured static types catching ~15% of real JavaScript defects at compile time; Nagappan et al. (2008) found test-first cut pre-release defect density 40–90% across four industrial teams; Boehm & Basili (2001) quantified how sharply defect cost climbs the later it's caught.

authdepth.title: Five locks between a stolen cookie and your account
authdepth.subtitle: Authentication is server-proxied Firebase — then four more independent layers that each assume the previous one already failed.

stepup.d: Sensitive actions demand a fresh 6-digit code: only its SHA-256 lands in Redis (10-min TTL); success mints a one-shot UUID consumed by atomic getAndDelete. Lockout ladder: 5 tries → 15-min cooldown → 3 cycles/24 h → HTTP 423.

fp.d: Every session is bound to HMAC-SHA256(IP + user-agent) under a dedicated key, compared in constant time — a cookie replayed from another machine dies on arrival. Fail-secure when missing.

travel.d: GeoIP gate with a 500 km/h cap and a 500 ms time budget — fails closed for admin and company roles. The full story is in the GeoIP card below.

revoke.d: The JWT carries a tokenVersion checked against Redis (~1-2 ms). Bump it and every device's next request gets HTTP 419 — sessions die mid-flight, no blacklist scans.

totp.d: The TOTP seed is Cloud-KMS-encrypted (totp-secrets-key); 10 backup codes are BCrypt-12 hashed then KMS-sealed; the 2FA flag re-arms on every admin login.

authdepth.enumDesc: Password reset answers identically for real and unknown emails — response time normalised (~500 ms ± jitter) outside the DB transaction, with a persisted 60-second cooldown. An attacker learns nothing, not even from the clock.
authdepth.snippetCaption: The 401 vs 419 contract — stale sessions refresh silently; only a real auth failure logs out.
authdepth.caveat: Honest: step-up tokens are SHA-256 + UUID in Redis (HMAC is used for consent cookies and session fingerprints, not step-up); security metrics currently log-only.

math.complexityTitle: Why a graph beats packing the codebase into a prompt
math.complexityBody: A k-hop question is O(k); nearest-neighbour retrieval is O(log n) — both with no attention cost. Stuffing the same answer into a prompt is O(n) and degrades in the middle of long context. The graph stays sharp where a context window blurs.

verdict.title: Contract-driven development — with drift moved to compile time
verdict.noRot: No hand-written mock or expectation to rot: the client is regenerated, never transcribed — the drift-through-duplication failure class is gone by construction.
verdict.staleFail: Tests import the same generated types as production, so a test cannot pass against a stale shape — the "passes in CI, fails in prod" gap closes at the type level.
verdict.runtime: What classic consumer-driven contracts add — verifying the running provider — is covered by the live-BE trace-equivalence tier and backend Testcontainers suites against real PostgreSQL and Redis. Best of both, not a shortcut.

techstack.whyHint: Click a layer to see why we chose it.

whys.frontend: Angular + strict TypeScript, because a two-repo product needs compile-time honesty; Tailwind + Material so three people ship consistent UI without a design department.
whys.backend: Boring on purpose: Spring Boot + Java 21 has an answer for everything — transactions, events, scheduling — and Liquibase keeps every schema change reviewable.
whys.data: PostgreSQL for facts, Redis (Sentinel) for speed, Firestore for off-host crown jewels, KMS + Secret Manager so storing keys is never our problem.
whys.infra: Each layer is replaceable: Cloudflare absorbs the noise, nginx + Docker keep the host simple, Ansible rebuilds the whole server from one command.
whys.observability: Logs are evidence: journald sealed at the source, shipped by Alloy to Loki on GCS — queryable for 30 days, tamper-evident the whole way.
whys.integrations: Money and identity stay with specialists — Stripe, Fakturownia (KSeF), Firebase, Meta — behind ports we can swap without touching business logic.

techstack.title: The stack at a glance
techstack.subtitle: Startup in the box, taken literally — the parts that usually keep a founder up at night are already solved. Your data is built to survive the worst day: PostgreSQL on OVH's managed tier, Firestore and Google Cloud Storage can each switch on point-in-time recovery, with daily OVH server backups alongside — options you enable once, so an outage never costs user data. Full internationalization across backend and frontend, paired with GDPR/RODO compliance, makes a new European market a configuration step, not a rewrite. And security is engineered in, not bolted on: HMAC-signed, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite session cookies; admin 2FA via Google Authenticator; step-up authentication with short-lived e-mail codes bound to a Redis-hashed IP and user-agent fingerprint — and more. So you can put your energy into the business, not into worrying whether it's safe.

logs.t: One log system for the whole team
logs.d: Structured logs — every line carries a unique request id and timestamp, GDPR-compliant — so Loki + Grafana alone cover per-endpoint performance, service health from the /health probes, and live monitoring: one system for admins, support and the SOC analyst.

cicd.failDetail: health probe fails → restore from immutable backup → green, Postgres volumes intact.
cicd.note: Pipeline verified in .github/workflows + .github/scripts. The GitHub-IP network gate is built (ipset) but staged — not yet wired.

subscription.title: 9-state subscription lifecycle
subscription.subtitle: An event-sourced finite-state machine. Every transition carries a guard and a trigger — and the backend is the single source of truth.
subscription.hint: Pick a scenario above and watch the token travel the real transitions.

trial.label: Trial → Enterprise
trial.caption: A Free company activates the Enterprise trial (guard: must be on Free); a successful Stripe checkout then converts it to a paid Enterprise plan.

payfail.label: Payment fails → recover
payfail.caption: A failed payment webhook parks the plan in PAYMENT_FAILED — remembering it — and a successful retry restores the exact plan it had before.

terms.label: Terms re-consent
terms.caption: A new Terms version parks the company in TERMS_PENDING, remembering its previous state (the dashed ring). Accept within the grace window and it resumes exactly where it was.

suspend.label: Grace expires → suspended
suspend.caption: If the grace window lapses, TermsGraceProcessorCronJob moves the company to SUSPENDED_LEGAL; prolonged non-compliance then closes the account.

downgrade.label: Downgrade
downgrade.caption: A downgrade request parks the plan in DOWNGRADE_PENDING; the period-end cron applies it when the paid period ends, dropping back to Free.

subscription.codeCaption: Terms re-consent remembers exactly where you were — and resumes there.

billing.title: Billing saga — Stripe to an invoice, exactly once
billing.subtitle: A Stripe webhook becomes a Fakturownia invoice (bridged to KSeF) through an after-commit saga, with idempotency at three layers — so a payment is invoiced once, never twice, never zero times.
billing.idemIntro: Stripe can deliver checkout.session.completed and invoice.paid for one payment — and retry either. Three layers guarantee a single invoice.

idem.fast: Fast-path — skip the work if the Stripe event id was already handled (non-blocking).
idem.db: The real guard — a DB unique constraint; a concurrent duplicate raises DataIntegrityViolationException, caught as "already processed".
idem.provider: Provider-level — Fakturownia's oid_unique refuses a second invoice for the same payment.

billing.codeCaption: From subscription/stripe + subscription/event. The platform runs in production; payments are the one piece we kept back — on staging this whole pipeline ran end-to-end, invoices generated and delivered, suites green. Switching invoicing on (and emitting to KSeF) is one flag in the Fakturownia API call. In this demo everything stays in test mode — nothing is charged.

instagram.title: Instagram & Meta — a real OAuth integration, not a logo
instagram.subtitle: Influencers connect their account through Instagram Business Login — the same OAuth 2.0 flow Meta certifies Tech Providers for, wired end to end.
instagram.provider: Meta Tech Provider · Instagram Business Login

facts.secret: The client_secret never leaves the server — the browser only ever sees an authorization code.
facts.redact: Every log line is scrubbed: access_token=[redacted], so a token can't leak into logs.
facts.redirect: redirect_uri is validated; a mismatch is rejected with a clear REDIRECT_URI_MISMATCH error.
facts.validator: A startup validator checks the Meta app config before serving traffic — Instagram Business Login added, app token valid.

instagram.kmsTitle: Encrypted at rest with Google Cloud KMS
instagram.kmsDesc: The access token is stored only as KMS ciphertext — the key lives in Google Cloud KMS, never in the database. Steal the database and the token is useless. Admins' TOTP 2FA secrets get the same protection, under their own key.
instagram.kmsMeta: AES-256-GCM · key ring instagram-tokens · europe-central2 (Warsaw) · validated at startup, GDPR-audited
instagram.codeCaption: From auth/social/instagram/InstagramService.java — the real token exchange. In this demo the connect button is impression-only; the live flow runs in production.

consent.title: Court-defensible consent — proof a human clicked
consent.subtitle: Every acceptance captures the browser's trusted-event flag, the screen coordinates and a hash of the exact document version — then HMAC-SHA256-signs the bundle.

facts.grace: Versioned documents with a unique (type, language, version) key and a 38-day re-consent grace window.
facts.header: Clients learn what to re-accept via an X-Consent-Required: TYPE:version header.
facts.softblock: Stale consent soft-blocks only new commitments (POST campaign / apply) — browsing and profile stay open.
facts.audit: Every personal-data touch emits a structured GDPR audit line with the email pre-masked (j***@example.com).

consent.codeCaption: isTrusted is false for any element.click() — so a stored true is hard evidence of a physical click.
consent.note: This HMAC signs the consent cookie, the Meta deletion callback and the session fingerprint — distinct from step-up auth (SHA-256(code)+UUID via Redis). Illustrative; the demo signs nothing real.

geoip.title: Impossible travel — a login can't outrun a plane
geoip.subtitle: If a session jumps between two places faster than anyone could physically travel, the move is impossible — so the session is challenged before an attacker can use a stolen cookie.

tiers.samecity: Same city — or within 50 km in the same country — is allowed without a speed check.
tiers.samecountry: Same country, farther apart: speed = great-circle distance ÷ time; over 500 km/h is impossible.
tiers.crosscountry: A different country inside a 10-minute window is always blocked — no speed maths needed.

geoip.riskNote: The 0–100 score powers the admin risk-analysis endpoint; live sessions enforce the same signals through a fast boolean impossible-travel gate.

db.maxmind: MaxMind license API — auto-download, weekly refresh
db.gcs: GCS bucket + Firestore lock — one node licenses, others pull

geoip.cbUser: Normal users → fail open by design (availability first) — the impossible-travel gate degrades gracefully.
geoip.cbAdmin: Admins & companies → fail closed after 5 failures — security first.
geoip.codeCaption: From common/security/geoip + SessionSecurityService. 500 km/h is the enforced threshold; the speed and geo signals run on the bundled GeoLite2 DB, with VPN/Tor enrichment available on the licensed MaxMind edition. The demo geolocates nothing.

gdpr.title: GDPR / RODO — compliance built into the code, not bolted on
gdpr.subtitle: Consent is provable, forgetting is real, and every personal-data touch is logged with the personal data masked out.
gdpr.badgeSub: data-subject rights wired end to end

consent.d: An HMAC-signed cookie carries the isTrusted browser flag, the document hash and screen coords — court-defensible proof a human accepted a specific version.

grace.d: A new Terms version starts a configurable countdown — 38 days by default, set per app — and ConsentEnforcementCronJob then blocks accounts that haven't re-consented.

audit.d: Every access emits a structured GDPR: line — actor, purpose, legal basis — with the email masked to j***@example.com.

meta.d: signed request verified, then queued or run

zerotrust.title: Beyond zero trust — defence in depth, verified at every hop
zerotrust.subtitle: A request crosses seven trust boundaries from the edge to the immutable core. No layer trusts the one before it; privileged actions need a hardware key; the core cannot be modified at all.

principles.hardware: Hardware root of trust for admin

edge.title: Cloudflare edge
edge.detail: DDoS scrubbing, WAF and real client IP — and post-quantum hybrid TLS negotiated at the edge.

net.title: Host firewall
net.detail: Default-DROP iptables; SYN-flood and port-scan throttling before a packet reaches a port.

web.title: nginx gateway
web.detail: Six $real_ip zones, a 403 wall for scanner user-agents (sqlmap, nmap…), coarse 429 rate-zones.

redis.title: Redis rate-limit
redis.detail: Per-identity sliding-window limiter; circuit-breaker falls back to memory; keys GDPR-anonymised, 24 h retention. Sentinel HA, fail-fast.

app.title: Application identity
app.detail: Firebase auth, session binding, GeoIP impossible-travel (fails closed for admins) and step-up for sensitive actions.

admin.title: Admin / break-glass
admin.detail: Operator host access requires a hardware security key (sk-ssh-ed25519, touch-to-verify); root is per-command sudoers, never a shell.

core.title: Immutable core
core.detail: Deployed artefacts locked with chattr +i, secrets sealed, audit append-only — nothing on disk is trusted or writable.

zerotrust.note: Post-quantum hybrid key exchange is negotiated at the Cloudflare edge; the origin link runs hardened TLS 1.3. Every layer maps to real config in deployment/ and application-prod.yml — drawn as architecture, fired by nothing in this demo.

admin-2fa.title: Admin sign-in with 2FA
admin-2fa.tagline: Log in as the admin — with a phone in hand. The first code will be wrong on purpose.
admin-2fa.proves: Admins get mandatory TOTP; a stolen password alone is useless.

steps.login: You are the admin — this is the standard sign-in screen. In the sandbox you do not need to type anything; let us get to the codes.
steps.first-code: The server wants a TOTP code. That is the admin phone in the corner — generate the first one.
steps.first-code-refused: The code is on the phone. Look at it, then send it to the server — and watch what comes back.
steps.fresh-code: The first code expired before it could be used — that is real TOTP behaviour: the window is seconds. Generate a fresh one.
steps.signed-in: This one is current. Send it — the dialog closes and the admin is in.

recap.f1: Admins don't get a choice: TOTP 2FA is mandatory, enforced server-side.
recap.f2: A stale code is rejected exactly like a wrong one — the window is seconds, not minutes.
recap.f3: In production the seed is KMS-encrypted and backup codes are BCrypt-hashed.

stepup-email.title: Change the account e-mail
stepup-email.tagline: A sensitive action asks you to prove it's really you — a fresh code, right now.
stepup-email.proves: Step-up re-auth guards the actions that matter; sessions alone aren't trusted.

steps.change-email: These are the company's account settings. Enter any new e-mail address and send the verification email.
steps.enter-code: The platform won't just trust the session — a one-time code went to the verified address. Check the inbox in the corner and type it in.
steps.saved: The code went through, so the change is under way: a confirmation link has gone to the new address and clicking it is what finishes the job. And here is a product decision: companies share accounts, so everyday actions need only a session — but sensitive ones ask for fresh proof. That is our answer to 2FA for shared accounts.

recap.f1: Sensitive actions re-authenticate: a fresh code, single-use, minutes-long TTL.
recap.f2: Only the code's SHA-256 ever touches Redis; success mints a one-shot token consumed atomically.
recap.f3: Shared company accounts stay safe: the dangerous switches sit behind fresh proof.

company-campaign.title: Run a campaign
company-campaign.tagline: Create a campaign, watch an influencer apply, and decide — the whole lifecycle from the company chair.
company-campaign.proves: The marketplace core: real forms, real states, one coherent flow.

steps.create-campaign: A campaign brief is one form. Fill it in — the internal name, the public title, where you are meeting, and what you want from the creator.
steps.publish-campaign: The form is complete, so the publish button has come alive. Publish it — the campaign gets a page of its own.
steps.campaign-live: This is the published campaign: the public title, the location and the brief, exactly as a creator will see it.
steps.decide-applicant: Once published, a campaign starts collecting applications right away. These are your campaign's applicants: decide on Ola's application — accept it or pass.
steps.lifecycle: Accepted — the collaboration moved to In Progress. Every state you've just walked is the same machine the survey draws.

recap.f1: One coherent lifecycle: draft → published → applications → in progress — no orphan states.
recap.f2: Your campaign persisted in the in-browser store — create and edit work like production.
recap.f3: The same data feeds both sides: switch to the influencer sandbox to see her view.

influencer-collab.title: Land a collaboration
influencer-collab.tagline: Browse campaigns, apply, get accepted — the same marketplace from the creator's side.
influencer-collab.proves: Two-sided by design: the same data, two honest perspectives.

steps.browse: You're Ola now — a creator. These are real campaigns from companies. Open one that suits you.
steps.apply: Found something? Apply from the campaign's page — add a note if you like.
steps.applied: The application is in. The company sees it on their applicant list straight away, and you have the confirmation here.
steps.accepted: Good news travels fast: the company has just accepted you. This is your applications view — the status is already green.

recap.f1: The same marketplace, the creator's chair: browse → apply → accepted.
recap.f2: Applications are real state transitions, not mailbox threads.
recap.f3: Run the company sandbox to sit on the other side of this exact flow.

nip-to-ksef.title: From NIP to KSeF
nip-to-ksef.tagline: Type a NIP, watch the company data arrive, verify your e-mail, hit plan limits, upgrade — and follow the invoice to KSeF.
nip-to-ksef.proves: Polish-market onboarding and billing, end to end, with no manual steps.

steps.nip-lookup: Company onboarding starts with one number. Type a NIP (try 5260250995) and search.
steps.company-confirmed: Everything arrived from the registries by itself — GUS, VAT status, PKD, even the bank account. Confirm the data.
steps.verify-mail: One thing left: prove the e-mail is yours. The branded mail just landed — open the inbox and click.
steps.activated: That click auto-activated the account — no human in the loop. You're on the plan page now: see the campaign limits per plan.
steps.upgrade: Need more room? Open the plan change — we show the price and the terms before you confirm anything.
steps.upgrade-terms: Before you pay — the subscription terms and the consent. Tick it; without it the payment button stays disabled.
steps.upgrade-confirm: Price, terms and consent in one place. The test card is already attached — confirm, and the payment and activation run themselves.
steps.invoice-sent: The payment succeeded, so the billing saga has already issued the invoice in Fakturownia. Send it on to KSeF — one click, one flag.
steps.ksef-done: And there it is — registered in the national e-invoice system, with its KSeF number.

recap.f1: Onboarding is one NIP: GUS/KRS data, VAT status and PKD arrive on their own.
recap.f2: E-mail verification auto-activates the account — no manual review queue.
recap.f3: Payment → invoice → KSeF is one saga; the demo's KSeF hop is the same single flag production flips.

support-ticket.title: Get help, fast
support-ticket.tagline: Something's wrong? File a ticket and watch the answer arrive — the support loop from the user's chair.
support-ticket.proves: Support is a built flow with reference codes and mail — not an inbox black hole.

steps.ticket-created: Something's not right? Describe it and send — you'll get a reference code on the spot.
steps.reference-issued: That is the ticket reference — keep it. In production the same number goes out by mail, so the conversation has one identifier on both sides.
steps.read-response: Support has already answered. This is your tickets view — open it and read the reply. In production a mail lands too, with the same reference.

recap.f1: Every ticket gets a reference code — trackable even without an account.
recap.f2: Replies thread on the ticket and go out by mail (the outbox pattern from the survey).
recap.f3: Run the admin sandbox to answer tickets from the other side.

admin-ops.title: Admin operations
admin-ops.tagline: A support ticket arrives; answer it and run a full GDPR cascade delete — by the book.
admin-ops.proves: Moderation and the right to be forgotten are real flows, not policy pages.

steps.admin-respond: This is the admin queue. Open a ticket and answer the user — your reply threads onto it instantly.
steps.reply-threaded: The reply is on the thread already — under the customer’s message, signed and dated. In production a mail goes out at the same moment, carrying the same reference.
steps.cascade-delete: Now the serious one: a GDPR erasure request. You are on the campaign it concerns — open the cascade delete.
steps.cascade-confirm: The counts in the preview are the real state of the database, not an estimate: records per system, and a warning for what cannot be undone. Confirm — the cascade runs through every layer.
steps.cascade-receipt: Exactly the number the preview promised, and an audit-archive entry nobody can delete. Read the receipt before you close it.
steps.by-the-book: The cascade ran through Postgres, Firestore and Storage in one orchestrated flow — the campaign is gone from the marketplace, and the audit trail remains. That's GDPR as engineering.

recap.f1: Admin replies thread onto tickets and notify the user by mail.
recap.f2: Erasure is a previewed cascade — exact counts per system, and the delete itself has to echo the preview’s one-time code, so no blind DELETE gets through.
recap.f3: Every deletion leaves a masked audit trail; the data goes, the proof stays.
